Routing: Routing defines how an application responds to client requests at specific endpoints (URIs) and HTTP methods. Express provides intuitive methods like app.get(), app.post(), and app.all() for route definition.
const express = require('express'); const app = express(); app.get('/', (req, res) => res.send('Home')); app.post('/api/users', (req, res) => res.status(201).json({ id: 1 }));
Middleware: Middleware functions execute in sequence during the request-response cycle, with access to the request and response objects. They can modify objects, end the cycle, or call the next middleware via next().
const logger = (req, res, next) => { console.log(req.method, req.url); next(); }; app.use(logger); app.use(express.json());
App Setup: Setting up an Express app involves creating the app instance, configuring middleware, defining routes, and starting the server with app.listen(). Includes error handling middleware defined last.
const express = require('express'); const app = express(); const PORT = process.env.PORT || 3000; app.use(express.json()); app.get('/', (req, res) => res.json({ status: 'OK' })); app.listen(PORT);

Built-in: Express includes built-in middleware: express.json() for JSON body parsing, express.urlencoded() for form data, express.static() for static files, and express.Router() for modular routing.
app.use(express.json({ limit: '10mb' })); app.use(express.urlencoded({ extended: false })); app.use(express.static('public', { maxAge: '1d' }));
Third-party: Third-party middleware adds cookie-parsing (cookie-parser), logging (morgan), compression (compression), CORS (cors), and session management (express-session).
const cors = require('cors'); const morgan = require('morgan'); app.use(cors({ origin: 'https://example.com' })); app.use(morgan('combined'));
Custom: Custom middleware encapsulates reusable logic for auth, validation, logging, or request transformation. A middleware function takes req, res, and next parameters.

const validateUser = (req, res, next) => { const { email, password } = req.body; if (!email || !password) return res.status(400).json({ error: 'Required' }); req.validated = { email, password }; next(); }; app.post('/login', validateUser, loginHandler);
Error Handling: Error-handling middleware has four parameters (err, req, res, next) and catches errors from preceding middleware and routes. Define it last in the middleware stack.
app.use((err, req, res, next) => { const status = err.status || 500; const message = err.message || 'Error'; console.error(err.stack); res.status(status).json({ error: message }); });

Router: Express Router enables modular, mountable route handlers. Routers act as mini-applications with their own middleware and routes, keeping code organized by feature.

const router = express.Router(); router.use(authMiddleware); router.get('/', (req, res) => res.json([{ id: 1 }])); router.post('/', (req, res) => res.status(201).json(req.body)); module.exports = router; app.use('/api/users', userRouter);
Route Params: Route parameters capture values from the URL path. They are defined with a colon prefix and accessed via req.params. Params can be optional or use regex patterns.
app.get('/users/:userId', (req, res) => { const id = req.params.userId; res.json({ userId: id }); }); app.get('/files/:filename(\\.png)', handler);
Query Strings: Query strings pass key-value pairs after the ? in the URL. Express parses them and makes them available via req.query. Useful for filtering, pagination, and search parameters.
app.get('/api/users', (req, res) => { const { page = 1, limit = 10, sort } = req.query; const skip = (page - 1) * limit; res.json({ page, limit, sort }); });

Headers: Request headers are accessed via req.headers. Response headers are set with res.set() or res.header(). CORS headers, content negotiation, and caching are common use cases.
app.use((req, res, next) => { res.header('X-Powered-By', 'Express'); res.header('Access-Control-Allow-Origin', '*'); next(); }); const userAgent = req.headers['user-agent'];
Body Parsing: Express can parse various request body formats: JSON (express.json()), URL-encoded form data (express.urlencoded()), raw text, and multipart file uploads (multer).

app.use(express.json()); app.use(express.urlencoded({ extended: true })); const multer = require('multer'); const upload = multer({ dest: 'uploads/' }); app.post('/upload', upload.single('file'), (req, res) => res.json(req.file));
File Upload: File uploads in Express use the multer middleware. Multer handles multipart/form-data and provides file metadata including original name, size, mimetype, and temp file path.

const storage = multer.diskStorage({ destination: './uploads', filename: (req, file, cb) => cb(null, Date.now() + '-' + file.originalname) }); const upload = multer({ storage, limits: { fileSize: 5e6 } }); app.post('/profile', upload.single('avatar'), handler);

Pug: Pug (formerly Jade) is a template engine for Express with terse syntax using indentation instead of tags. It supports variables, conditionals, iteration, mixins, and layout inheritance.
app.set('view engine', 'pug'); app.set('views', './views'); // views/index.pug: doctype html html head title= title body h1 Welcome #{name}
EJS: EJS (Embedded JavaScript) uses plain HTML with <% %> tags for logic and <%= %> for output. It includes partials, layouts via express-ejs-layouts, and supports async rendering.

app.set('view engine', 'ejs'); app.set('views', './views'); // views/index.ejs:

Welcome <%= name %>

<% if (user) { %>

Logged in

<% } %>
Handlebars: Handlebars is a logic-less template engine with {{mustache}} syntax. It enforces strict separation of logic from presentation using helpers and partials instead of inline code.

const exphbs = require('express-handlebars'); app.engine('handlebars', exphbs()); app.set('view engine', 'handlebars'); // views/index.handlebars:

Welcome {{name}}

MongoDB: Integrating MongoDB with Express uses Mongoose ODM for schemas, models, and validation. Mongoose provides a schema-based solution for modeling application data.

const mongoose = require('mongoose'); mongoose.connect(process.env.MONGO_URI); const User = mongoose.model('User', { name: String, email: String }); app.get('/users', async (req, res) => res.json(await User.find()));
SQL/Prisma: Prisma ORM integrates with Express for type-safe database access. It supports PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, and SQL Server with auto-generated query client.

const { PrismaClient } = require('@prisma/client'); const prisma = new PrismaClient(); app.get('/users/:id', async (req, res) => { const user = await prisma.user.findUnique({ where: { id: Number(req.params.id) }, include: { posts: true } }); res.json(user); });
Redis: Redis with Express is used for caching, session storage, and rate limiting. Connect-redis stores Express sessions in Redis for fast, persistent session management.

const session = require('express-session'); const RedisStore = require('connect-redis')(session); const redis = require('redis'); const client = redis.createClient(); app.use(session({ store: new RedisStore({ client }), secret: 'secret', resave: false, saveUninitialized: false }));

JWT: JSON Web Tokens (JWT) provide stateless authentication. After login, a signed token containing user claims is sent to the client, which includes it in the Authorization header for protected routes.

const jwt = require('jsonwebtoken'); const token = jwt.sign({ userId: user.id, role: user.role }, process.env.JWT_SECRET, { expiresIn: '24h' }); const verifyToken = (req, res, next) => { const token = req.headers.authorization?.split(' ')[1]; try { req.user = jwt.verify(token, process.env.JWT_SECRET); next(); } catch (e) { res.status(401).json({ error: 'Invalid token' }); } };
Sessions: Express-session creates server-side sessions stored in memory or external stores like Redis. A signed cookie identifies the session, keeping user data on the server for security.

const session = require('express-session'); app.use(session({ secret: process.env.SESSION_SECRET, resave: false, saveUninitialized: true, cookie: { secure: true, httpOnly: true, maxAge: 86400000 } })); app.get('/login', (req, res) => { req.session.userId = user.id; res.redirect('/'); });
Passport: Passport.js provides strategy-based authentication supporting local, OAuth (Google, GitHub, Facebook), JWT, and many other providers. serializeUser/deserializeUser manage session persistence.

const passport = require('passport'); const LocalStrategy = require('passport-local'); passport.use(new LocalStrategy(async (username, password, done) => { const user = await User.findOne({ username }); if (!user || !user.verifyPassword(password)) return done(null, false); return done(null, user); })); app.post('/login', passport.authenticate('local', { successRedirect: '/', failureRedirect: '/login' }));

Best Practices: REST API best practices include proper HTTP methods and status codes, consistent naming (plural nouns), versioning, pagination, filtering, sorting, and comprehensive error responses.

const sendSuccess = (res, data, status = 200) => res.status(status).json({ success: true, data }); const sendError = (res, message, status = 400) => res.status(status).json({ success: false, error: message });
Versioning: API versioning prevents breaking changes from affecting existing clients. Common strategies include URL-based (/api/v1/), header-based (Accept-Version), and query-parameter versioning.

const v1 = express.Router(); const v2 = express.Router(); v1.get('/users', (req, res) => res.json({ version: 'v1' })); v2.get('/users', (req, res) => res.json({ version: 'v2' })); app.use('/api/v1', v1); app.use('/api/v2', v2);
Documentation: API documentation with Swagger/OpenAPI defines endpoints, schemas, and auth. Swagger UI provides interactive documentation. JSDoc comments auto-generate OpenAPI specs.

const swaggerJsdoc = require('swagger-jsdoc'); const swaggerUi = require('swagger-ui-express'); const specs = swaggerJsdoc({ definition: { openapi: '3.0.0', info: { title: 'My API', version: '1.0.0' } }, apis: ['./routes/*.js'] }); app.use('/api-docs', swaggerUi.serve, swaggerUi.setup(specs));

Socket.io Integration: Socket.io enables real-time bidirectional communication between the server and clients. Express apps integrate Socket.io by wrapping the HTTP server and attaching socket handlers with namespace support.

const http = require('http'); const { Server } = require('socket.io'); const server = http.createServer(app); const io = new Server(server, { cors: { origin: '*' } }); io.on('connection', (socket) => { console.log('User connected'); socket.on('message', (data) => io.emit('message', data)); socket.on('disconnect', () => console.log('Disconnected')); }); server.listen(3000);
ws Library: The ws library is a lightweight WebSocket implementation for Express. It attaches to the HTTP server and provides a simple event-based API with support for rooms and binary data.

const { WebSocketServer } = require('ws'); const server = app.listen(3000); const wss = new WebSocketServer({ server }); wss.on('connection', (ws) => { ws.on('message', (data) => wss.clients.forEach(client => client.send(data))); ws.send('Connected'); });
Broadcasting: Socket.io rooms and namespaces organize connections into logical groups for targeted broadcasting. The broadcast flag sends to all clients except the sender, and rooms isolate groups.

io.on('connection', (socket) => { socket.join('room-' + userId); socket.broadcast.to('room-' + userId).emit('user-online', userId); io.to('room-' + userId).emit('notification', { text: 'New message' }); });

Helmet: Helmet secures Express apps by setting various HTTP headers including Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, X-XSS-Protection, Strict-Transport-Security, and X-Content-Type-Options.
const helmet = require('helmet'); app.use(helmet()); app.use(helmet.contentSecurityPolicy({ directives: { defaultSrc: ["'self'"], scriptSrc: ["'self'", "'unsafe-inline'"] } }));
Rate Limiting: express-rate-limit protects against brute-force attacks by limiting repeated requests from the same IP. Rate limits are configurable per window with custom messages and headers.

const rateLimit = require('express-rate-limit'); const limiter = rateLimit({ windowMs: 15 * 60 * 1000, max: 100, standardHeaders: true, legacyHeaders: false, message: { error: 'Too many requests' } }); app.use('/api/', limiter);
Compression: compression middleware reduces response size using gzip/deflate. It automatically compresses JSON, text, and other compressible responses, improving bandwidth usage and load times.
const compression = require('compression'); app.use(compression({ threshold: 0, level: 6 })); // Skip compression for small SSE or already-compressed responses
Input Validation: Input validation libraries like Joi, express-validator, or Zod prevent injection attacks and malformed data. Validation middleware sanitizes and validates request bodies, params, and queries.

const { body, validationResult } = require('express-validator'); app.post('/user', [ body('email').isEmail().normalizeEmail(), body('age').isInt({ min: 0 }) ], (req, res) => { const errors = validationResult(req); if (!errors.isEmpty()) return res.status(400).json({ errors: errors.array() }); });
